In short these cumulative mass and density function (distribution but less used) is just another way of visualizing the distribution (@sec-distribution) of a quantative variable (@sec-quantitative-variable) although it could aso be used for ordinal variable (@sec-qualitative-variable). The term mass is used when talking about discrete quantative and the density for continuous density, although it stems from more theoretical, it is easier to understand from a data-driven. If f1,f2, f3 are the frequency, in the cumulative version is c1 = f1, c2 = f1 + f2, c3 = f1 + f2 + f3. To reiterate, it is the same thing, and it contains the same information. You construct the cs from the fs and recover the fs from the cs.

Cummulative for ordinal
```{r}

df_dist <- data.frame(
        size = c("Asmall", "Bmedium", "Clarge"),
        value = c(4, 2, 3))

fig1 <- ggplot(dat = df_dist, aes(x = size,  y = value, fill = size)) +
    geom_col()+
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Asmall" = "orange",
                                "Bmedium" = "purple",
                                "Clarge" = "#69b3a2")) +
    ylim(c(0, 11)) +
    theme_bw()


 df_cumul <- data.frame(
    cumul = c("Asmall <=", "Bmedium <=","Bmedium <=", "Clarge <=", "Clarge <=",  "Clarge <="),
    size = c("Asmall", "Asmall", "Bmedium", "Asmall", "Bmedium", "Clarge"),
    value = c(4, 4, 2, 4, 2, 3)
 )

fig2 <- ggplot(dat = df_cumul, aes(x = cumul, y = value, fill = size)) +
    geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Asmall" = "orange",
                                "Bmedium" = "purple",
                                "Clarge" = "#69b3a2")) +
    ylim(c(0, 11)) +
    theme_bw()

fig <- fig1 + fig2 +
    plot_layout(axis_titles = "collect", guides = "collect")
fig
```


And cumulative for quantitative.

```{r}
# 1. Generate random sample data
set.seed(42)
data_values <- rnorm(100)

hist(data_values, col = "lightblue" )

# 2. Compute the initial histogram without plotting it
hist_object <- hist(data_values, plot = FALSE)

# 3. Replace the standard bin counts with cumulative counts
hist_object$counts <- cumsum(hist_object$counts)

# 4. Plot the cumulative histogram
plot(hist_object,
     main = "Cumulative Histogram (Base R)",
     xlab = "Values",
     ylab = "Cumulative Frequency",
     col = "lightblue")

```



## Formal {.unnumbered}

For grouping, if there are b_i bins,
$N(i) = \sum_{j = 0}^i n(b_j)$

or we can use frequency
$F(i) = \sum_{j = 0}^i f(b_j)$

where x in b_j does not belong is other b_j, and y in b_j is smaller than x in b_k if k is smaller than j.

<!-- In the formal definition, a cumulative is split into two cases where the variable is discrete or continuous. The discrete case is called a cumulative mass function (cmf) and the continuous case is called a cumulative density function (cdf). The two are unified under the term cumulative distribution function (cdf). -->

there is an alternate definition, which does not require bining and works directly from the values.

$N(x) = \sum_{x_i \le x} n(x_i)$


To focus on the applied is simply
$F(x) = \sum_{x_i \le x} f(x_i)$


where fX is the frequency of the value xi. In other words, it is the sum of all frequency that are less than or equal to x.


An immediate consequence is always increasing.

## Examples {.unnumbered}

And example of cumulative for discrete, the scale on y-axis is changed so we can see that the one the right is the one the left that is gradualy stacked
```{r}

# Quantitative
set.seed(1)
df_discrete <- data.frame(
    size = rpois(100, 5)) |>
    count(size)

fig_discrete <- ggplot(df_discrete, aes(x = size, xend = size, y = 0, yend = n)) +
 geom_point(aes(x = size, y = n)) +
  geom_segment() +
  ylim(c(0, 100)) +
  theme_bw()

df_discrete_cumulative <- cumsum(df_discrete)
fig_discrete_cumulative <- ggplot(df_discrete_cumulative, aes(x = size, xend = size, y = 0, yend = n)) +
 geom_point(aes(x = size, y = n)) +
  geom_segment() +
  theme_bw()

fig_cumDiscrete <- fig_discrete + fig_discrete_cumulative +
    plot_layout(axis_titles = "collect")

fig_cumDiscrete
```

Here are example of three distribution, a flat/uniform, a highly asymmetric distributiona and a symmetric

Uniform

```{r}
set.seed(42)

hist(data_values, col = "lightblue")

```


Exponential
```{r}

set.seed(42)
data_values <- rexp(100, 1)

hist(data_values, col = "lightblue")

# 2. Compute the initial histogram without plotting it
hist_object <- hist(data_values, plot = FALSE)

# 3. Replace the standard bin counts with cumulative counts
hist_object$counts <- cumsum(hist_object$counts)

# 4. Plot the cumulative histogram
plot(hist_object,
     main = "Cumulative Histogram (Base R)",
     xlab = "Values",
     ylab = "Cumulative Frequency",
     col = "lightblue")

```

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- Cumulative distribution are very convenient when one wants to know the @sec-median and @sec-quantile of a given distribution.
- Cumulative distribution is essential when working with distribution. For instance, if we want to compare two distribution.
- Easy for statisticians to work on increasing function
- Why it won't work for qualitative, because the order on x-axis is not relevant, so there won't be a unique. Although, ordinal variable is okay.
- It is often better to work with frequency of proportion than row number so the range on the y value is from 0 to 1.



<!-- In advanced mathematical statistics, textbooks clarify a common terminological distinction before providing rigorous definitions:
Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) is the unifying, mathematically precise term for the "cumulative density and mass distribution" of any random variable.
Probability Mass Function (PMF) applies strictly to discrete variables.
Probability Density Function (PDF) applies strictly to continuous variables.

Here are the rigorous definitions from two universally cited textbooks in mathematical statistics.

1. The Unifying Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)
The CDF completely determines the probability distribution of a random variable, regardless of whether it is discrete or continuous.

Textbook Source
Book: Statistical Inference (2nd Edition, 2002)
Authors: George Casella and Roger L. Berger
Publisher: Duxbury / Thomson Learning

The Definition
In Chapter 1 ("Probability Theory"), Casella and Berger define the cumulative distribution function of a random variable X:
Definition 1.5.1: "The cumulative distribution function of a random variable X, denoted by FX(x), is defined by

$F_X(x) = P_X(X \le x), \quad \text{for all } x.$

[...] The abbreviation cdf will be used to denote cumulative distribution function."


Rigorous Mathematical Properties of a CDF
For FX(x) to be a valid cumulative distribution function, it must satisfy three rigorous mathematical properties:


1.Monotonicity: It is nondecreasing; if x $x_1 < x_2 \implies F_X(x_1) \le F_X(x_2)$

2. Limits: $\lim_{x \to -\infty} F_X(x) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x \to \infty} F_X(x) = 1$

3. Continuity: It is right-continuous; for every x $\lim_{x \to x_0^+} F_X(x) = F_X(x_0)$


1. The Discrete Case: Probability Mass Function (PMF)
When dealing with a discrete variable, the cumulative distribution accumulates point probabilities.

Textbook Source
Book: Introduction to Mathematical Statistics (8th Edition, 2019)
Authors: Robert V. Hogg, Joseph W. McKean, and Allen T. Craig
Publisher: Pearson

The Definition
In Chapter 1 ("Probability and Distributions"), Hogg, McKean, and Craig formalize the discrete case:
"Let X be a discrete random variable with space D. The probability mass function (pmf) of X is defined by

$p_X(x) = P(X = x), \quad \text{for } x \in \mathcal{D}$


and pX(x)=0 otherwise."

The Mass Distribution Relation
The cumulative mass distribution is achieved by summing these discrete points up to a value x:

$F_X(x) = \sum_{x_i \le x} p_X(x_i)$

1. The Continuous Case: Probability Density Function (PDF)
When dealing with a continuous variable, probability at a single point is zero, requiring calculus to evaluate a cumulative range.

Textbook Source
Book: Introduction to Mathematical Statistics (8th Edition, 2019) — Same Source

The Definition
Hogg, McKean, and Craig define the continuous random variable and its underlying density function:
"We say a random variable X is a continuous random variable if its cumulative distribution function FX(x) is continuous for all x∈R. [...] The probability density function (pdf) of X is a function fX(x) such that

$F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t) \, dt$
for all x∈R.


By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, at points where fX
(x) is continuous,
$f_X(x) = \frac{d}{dx}F_X(x)$."

The Density Distribution Relation

The cumulative density distribution is achieved by integrating the density function:
$P(a \le X \le b) = \int_{a}^{b} f_X(x) \, dx = F_X(b) - F_X(a)$

Conceptual Summary
"Mass" (PMF): Used for countable outcomes. The cumulative mass function looks like a stair-step graph because probability jumps up only at distinct, specific numbers.
"Density" (PDF): Used for continuous measurements. The cumulative density function is a smooth, unbroken curve because probability is spread continuously over an interval of real numbers. -->
